source.title: Detecting Trojaned DNNs Using Counterfactual Attributions
source.authors: Karan Sikka; Indranil Sur; Anirban Roy; Ajay Divakaran; Susmit Jha

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes neuron attributions in trained image classifiers using counterfactual attribution and neuron excitation, rather than reproducing the original neuron-analysis method.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly characterizes Trojan-related ghost neurons as poly-semantic and reports attribution evidence for trigger patterns and other image content. Detector AUC results, including results broken down by architecture, measure Trojan-detection performance rather than the prevalence or meaning of polysemantic neurons, so they are not rows. Results cited from other work are also excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper's main results are Trojan-detector AUCs. 'Poly-semantic' ghost neurons serve as a motivating observation and a tool for detection. The neuron evidence is one unnamed model, shown qualitatively (Figs. 3, 5). The trigger feature is deliberately implanted by data poisoning, so any mixed response is induced rather than arising naturally. Fig. 3 measures attribution toward the target class on clean and poisoned inputs. That fits a neuron which simply encodes the target class and is hijacked by the trigger, so it cannot show that unrelated inputs drive the neuron. No rate or prevalence of polysemantic neurons is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that Trojan behaviour is localized in a few poly-semantic ghost neurons that fire for both class content and the trigger. Counterfactual attributions on clean inputs can find these neurons, and exciting them reveals Trojaned models. Their detector (TrinityAI) improves on prior methods, by about 10% on harder TrojAI rounds.
record.recipe_differences: Uses counterfactual attributions and incremental neuron excitation to detect Trojaned models; it does not reproduce the original neuron-analysis method.

fits_no_version.finding: In backdoored image classifiers, a few penultimate-layer 'ghost' neurons carry the implanted trigger and also have high attribution toward the target class on clean inputs. Heatmaps show attribution on both the trigger and other image regions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Backdoor triggers implanted by data poisoning are encoded in a few neurons that also contribute to the target class on clean inputs (mixed trigger/class neurons in Trojaned models).

record.problems: The neuron-level evidence is qualitative and illustrative, with no reported frequency across models or quantitative neuron-level uncertainty. The example model and neuron are not named, and the paper does not test whether the mixed patterns share a feature used by the network.
record.rows_left_out: Detector AUC results, including the architecture and trigger-type breakdowns, are omitted because they report detector performance rather than neuron polysemanticity (Sections 5.2–5.3, Tables 1–2).

untested.parts: Natural (non-implanted) polysemantic neurons in vision classifiers, InceptionV1, prevalence, and whether the mixed inputs are unrelated.
All; Theorem 1 concerns concentration of trigger attributions, not superposition.
All; the architecture breakdown in Table 2 reports detector AUC, not the share of polysemantic neurons.

record.verdict_notes: Downgraded from the reader's tests/T2 with a V1 'supports' label. The 'poly-semantic' characterization is an untested interpretation used to motivate the method. The behaviour stems from a deliberately implanted trigger, and the evidence is qualitative from one unnamed model. Zoom In is cited ([40]) only for shortcut pathways across layers.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test the named InceptionV1 neuron, quantify how common this behavior is across vision models, or establish that the mixed patterns are unrelated in the network's learned representation.
Language models and transformer MLP neurons.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons, or by superposition.
Polysemanticity from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.
The share of polysemantic neurons across activation functions, architectures, or regularization choices, and the associated performance cost.
Whether apparently mixed inputs share a feature actually used by the network, or whether better tools show that the mixtures are coherent jobs.
How the measured prevalence of polysemanticity depends on activation range or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.subject: Trojaned DNN (example shown; model name not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Compared neuron attributions for predicting the target class across clean and poisoned inputs.

conditions.value: clean and poisoned examples; dataset and trigger type not stated

rows.measure: Neuron attribution for the target class
rows.value: The neurons associated with Trojan behavior have high counterfactual attribution on clean inputs as well as high attribution on poisoned inputs.
rows.note: The paper describes these ghost neurons as firing for patterns corresponding to both the actual class(es) and the trigger. The example model and neurons are not identified by name.
rows.check: Measures penultimate-neuron attribution for the target class on clean vs poisoned inputs (Fig. 3). High attribution on both does not show the neuron responds to unrelated natural features. The trigger is deliberately implanted, the model is unnamed, and no numbers are given.

rows.note: The authors interpret this as evidence of poly-semanticity; the paper does not identify the other image parts as unrelated features.
rows.check: A single qualitative heatmap (Fig. 5) for one ghost neuron in an unnamed backdoored model. 'Other parts of the images' are not identified as unrelated features, and the trigger response is induced by poisoning. It is an illustration supporting the detection method, not a test of V1.

relation.reason: The paper uses the poly-semantic ghost-neuron property for detection and does not test polysemanticity of natural features. It cites Zoom In [40] only to say ghost neurons can span layers.

tranche.reason: The main results are Trojan-detector AUCs. The ghost-neuron 'poly-semantic' property is used as a tool, so clean inputs can stand in for poisoned ones. Its only support is qualitative (Figs. 3, 5), and the trigger feature is induced on purpose.

source_check.notes: 'Poly-semantic' here means a penultimate-layer neuron fires for both class patterns and an implanted trigger. The evidence is qualitative (Figs. 3 and 5) on one unnamed model, and it does not show unrelated natural features.

statements.problem: None. It matches Observations 1-2, Fig. 3 and the contributions list. The evidence is qualitative, from one unnamed Trojaned model, and the trigger was implanted by poisoning.
